transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-26 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes | Attendees: Sarah (Redwood AE), Mark (Redwood SE), Priya (Ravenbrook Eng Lead), Tom (Ravenbrook CTO), Rachel (Ravenbrook Infra)

Summary: quick intake to understand viability for reserved capacity and how Ravenbrook expects to burst, and where Private/VPC would be required.

00:00 Sarah: Hey everyone thanks for jumping on, I think we have about 50 minutes carved out. Quick intros?
00:10 Priya: Hi Priya here, engineering lead on the inference team, we own the API surface that serves recommendations and search. Sorry for the background noise, I'm at a cafe.
00:18 Tom: Tom, CTO, joining from SFO.
00:22 Rachel: Rachel, infra, will talk deployment, security, network stuff.
00:27 Sarah: Awesome. Mark, SE from Redwood will cover ops and burst patterns.
00:31 Mark: Hey all.

02:05 Sarah: Priya can you sketch current stack — models, where you run them today, whether you use quantized variants, latency targets?
02:18 Priya: Sure. We're currently on a hosted provider for baseline traffic, mostly a 13B family open model with some smaller 6B for cheap calls. We do 8k context for the long form pipeline sometimes, but recommendations calls are usually short. We have a mix of quantized and fp16 in staging, but production is mostly fp16 on cloud endpoints.
02:45 Tom: Our p95 for recommend is about 180ms now, p99 is spiky up to 800ms during spikes. We want p95 < 200ms and p99 < 400ms ideally.
03:05 Mark: Got it. When you say spikes — are they predictable batch windows or ad hoc user surges?
03:12 Priya: Mostly ad hoc, e.g., product launches and internal experiments. There is also scheduled nightly batch reranks that can flood.

05:00 Sarah: What's your tolerance for preemption/eviction? If we put you on dedicated reserved nodes you can get lower preemption but hybrid strategies exist.
05:12 Rachel: We can't have core recommendation queries dropped. Eviction tolerance is low for user-facing calls, maybe acceptable for some background reranks.
05:25 Tom: We also have regulatory customers in EU where data residency matters — might need a VPC or Private deployment for those tenants.

07:10 Mark: So two axes — isolation for residency/compliance and capacity for burst. For isolation we can do reserved pools with tenant fencing, or a Private VPC deployment if you need the control plane on your side. Any preference?
07:30 Priya: Prefer staying on Redwood hosted for day-to-day but want a dedicated reserved pool to guarantee throughput. For the EU customers we might want a VPC or Private later.
07:45 Sarah: That makes sense — many customers start with Dedicated reserved pools + hosted fallback.

10:00 Priya: How does warm-pool/prewarmed node behavior work? We saw cold starts on other providers.
10:10 Mark: Redwood offers configurable warm pools. You can keep a percentage of GPUs prewarmed per model shard, and burst uses ephemeral nodes that can spin up. Warm nodes reduce token latency but add cost; we can show modeling.
10:35 Rachel: What about kernel selection and quantization — can you run 4-bit quantized JIT for the 13B to squeeze costs?
10:45 Mark: Yes, we have quantization profiles. Some customers run int4 and see 2-3x token cost reduction with modest latency differences. We'll add recommended profiles based on your workload.

13:40 Tom: Fallbacks — if reserved pool is saturated, can requests route to Redwood hosted as overflow? We need our app not to experience errors.
13:52 Sarah: Yes. Smart routing policy can overflow to hosted models or lower-cost variants; you can set hard/soft quotas per customer.
14:10 Priya: Important — on overflow the model outputs must be consistent, we care about regression. Any evals for divergence?
14:20 Mark: We do prompt set-based quality regression checks during rollout and can pin model variants. We'll run a small eval for your anchor prompts.

17:00 Rachel: Networking — will you provide VPC peering or do we open a bastion? Also KMS for key wrapping?
17:12 Sarah: For Dedicated we can support Private control plane + VPC peering. KMS/HSM integrations supported (AWS KMS, Vault). For hosted, we support customer-managed keys via envelope encryption.
17:32 Rachel: Audit logs and retention — SOC2 details?
17:38 Mark: We'll share the SOC2 report and the audit log retention add-on options.

21:00 Priya: Pricing shape question — how do you bill reserved pools vs warm-pool vs burst credits?
21:12 Sarah: Reserved pool is a monthly commit for the node hours; warm-pool carries a fractional baseline cost; burst credits are a metered per-minute or token-based charge for ephemeral usage. We'll send a tailored pricing sheet.
21:45 Tom: Need to org-justify costs — can you simulate cost for our qps profile?
21:52 Mark: Yes, send the hourly qps distribution and model mix, we can run a cost model and recommend node counts and warm-pool fractions.

25:30 Priya: SLA and latency guarantees?
25:36 Sarah: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed availability and latency best-effort targets; for strict latency SLOs we recommend Dedicated with warm-pools and colocated regions.
25:50 Tom: And rollback — can we do canary and automatic fallback?
25:56 Mark: Rollouts are supported: canary percentages, AB tests, and automatic fallback to previous model or hosted variant if error rates cross thresholds.

29:10 Rachel: Security controls — RBAC, SSO provisioning (SAML/Okta), token scopes?
29:18 Sarah: Yes to all; we integrate with Okta/SCIM, and provide fine-grained keys and route-level ACLs.
29:35 Rachel: Good. Also need encryption in transit and at rest — standards?
29:40 Mark: TLS + AES256 at rest; customer-managed KMS also available.

33:00 Priya: Operational concerns — how do you alert on queue buildup and p99 tail latency?
33:10 Mark: Console exposes per-route token and latency breakdowns. We also emit traces and alerts via webhook or PagerDuty. You can set SLA-based alarms.
33:30 Priya: Can you show retention windows for logs and prompt-level traces?
33:36 Mark: Logs retention configurable per account, we have a premium retention add-on.

36:20 Tom: Onboarding timeline — if we commit to a 6 month reserved pool what's the lead time to provision and test?
36:30 Sarah: Typical lead time 2-3 weeks for initial pool stand-up plus a week for migration and benchmarks. Private/VPC can take longer depending on network approvals.
36:45 Tom: We have a Q1 launch target for moving critical traffic to the reserved pool.
36:50 Sarah: That fits — plan a pilot in December/early January.

39:05 Priya: Benchmarks — we'd like p99 tail tests with our real prompts and some adversarial long context tests.
39:15 Mark: We'll run them in a deep-dive. We'll want your sample prompt set and traffic replay.
39:25 Priya: Ok we'll anonymize and send.

42:00 Sarah: Risks: cost overspend on warm pools vs latency breaches, model divergence on fallback, and EU compliance gating Private deployment. Anything to add?
42:12 Tom: Also concerned about multi-tenant blast radius — if another tenant spikes, can we ensure our reserved pool remains unaffected?
42:22 Mark: Reserved pools are isolated; we can allocate strict tenant fencing and QoS.

45:00 Rachel: One more — evictions during cloud preemption windows, do you guarantee node stickiness?
45:08 Mark: On Dedicated we avoid spot preemption; ephemeral burst nodes are best-effort. For guaranteed stickiness we recommend Reserved + warm-pool in a private placement.

47:30 Sarah: Recap and next steps — we'll send pricing, SOC2 + KMS docs, a proposed benchmark plan, and schedule a 90-minute technical deep dive. Priya you'll share traffic profile and prompt set.
47:50 Priya: Yep.
47:55 Tom: Sounds good.
48:05 Rachel: Thanks all.

48:30 Sarah: Action items quick readout: Mark will draft benchmark plan; Sarah will put pricing; Priya will send qps profile; Rachel will pull security contacts. We'll reconvene next week.

52:00 End of meeting.
